content: Ebola disease is caused by an infection with viruses belonging to the genus Orthoebolavirus. These viruses are primarily found in sub-Saharan Africa and are capable of causing severe and often fatal illnesses, with mortality rates reaching as high as 80 to 90 percent in some outbreaks. Among these viruses, the species Zaire orthoebolavirus has an FDA-approved vaccine available for prevention. Ebola disease was first identified in 1976 in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The viruses responsible for this disease are collectively referred to as orthoebolaviruses (formerly known as ebolaviruses). Without appropriate treatment, these viruses can lead to life-threatening conditions. There are four types of orthoebolaviruses known to cause disease in humans: 1. Ebola virus (species Orthoebolavirus zairense), which causes Ebola virus disease. 2. Sudan virus (species Orthoebolavirus sudanense), which causes Sudan virus disease. 3. Taï Forest virus (species Orthoebolavirus taiense), which causes Taï Forest virus disease. 4. Bundibugyo virus (species Orthoebolavirus bundibugyoense), which causes Bundibugyo virus disease. Other orthoebolaviruses, such as the Reston virus (species Orthoebolavirus restonense), can cause illness in nonhuman primates and pigs but not in humans. The Bombali virus (species Orthoebolavirus bombaliense) has been identified in bats, but it is not yet known whether it causes illness in animals or humans. The symptoms of Ebola disease typically begin with dry symptoms, such as fever, muscle aches, joint pain, and fatigue. As the disease progresses, wet symptoms often develop, including diarrhea, vomiting, and unexplained bleeding. The incubation period for Ebola disease ranges from 2 to 21 days after exposure to the virus, with symptoms most commonly appearing between 8 and 10 days. Individuals at the highest risk of contracting Ebola disease include healthcare providers and family members who care for infected individuals without proper infection control measures. For the general public and travelers, the risk of infection is low. Ebola disease is transmitted through direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person, whether they are alive or deceased. Bodily fluids that can transmit the virus include blood, saliva, sweat, urine, feces, vomit, breast milk, amniotic fluid, semen, and vaginal fluids. Rarely, the disease can also be transmitted through contact with infected animals, such as bats or primates. To prevent Ebola disease, individuals in or traveling to areas where the virus is present should avoid contact with bodily fluids from infected individuals or animals. This includes avoiding contaminated items such as clothing, bedding, needles, or medical equipment. Protective equipment should be worn when caring for someone with Ebola disease or handling their bodily fluids. Additionally, individuals returning from areas with active Ebola outbreaks should monitor their health for 21 days and seek medical attention immediately if symptoms develop. The FDA has approved a vaccine called ERVEBO® for the prevention of Ebola disease caused by Zaire orthoebolavirus. This vaccine is recommended for U.S. adults aged 18 years and older who are at risk of exposure to the virus. Diagnosis of Ebola disease is performed using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing to detect the virus's genetic material. Antibody testing may also be used. Patients suspected of having Ebola disease should be isolated in a healthcare facility until a definitive diagnosis is made. Treatment for Ebola disease includes two FDA-approved therapies: Inmazeb™ and Ebanga™, both of which are specifically effective against Zaire orthoebolavirus. Supportive care is critical for improving survival rates and includes administering fluids and electrolytes, managing blood pressure, controlling vomiting and diarrhea, reducing fever and pain, and treating any secondary infections that may arise.
